where: Section 3, paragraph on choosing a metric
problem: "pair it with latency so you do not scale out when servers are slow" gives the opposite of the usual rule. Slow servers under load are exactly when scale out is needed; latency is paired with RPS to avoid scaling out when the bottleneck is elsewhere (a slow database, a slow downstream API) and to avoid scaling in when RPS falls only because servers cannot accept work.
fix: "Requests per second shows arrival rate. Pair it with latency: high latency with high CPU and high RPS means scale out; high latency with low CPU and low RPS means the bottleneck is outside the group (a slow database or downstream service), so adding servers will not help."

problem: "ceil rounds up to the next whole server" is not exact; when L ÷ C is already a whole number (for example 900 ÷ 75 = 12) ceil leaves it unchanged rather than going to the next one.
fix: "ceil rounds a value up to the nearest whole number; a value that is already whole stays the same, so 12 stays 12."

where: Section 3, paragraph on metrics and failure modes
problem: "use per-instance metrics or a health check" mixes two different tools. A health check only tells you whether a server answers; it cannot show that one instance is hot while the average looks fine.
fix: "Average CPU can hide one hot instance. Use per-instance CPU metrics to find it; a health check only tells you whether a server responds, not whether it is overloaded."

problem: The saving is only valid if the off-peak load fits inside the 2-server minimum (2 × 60 = 120 requests per second). The example never states this, so a student may think the elastic group always keeps exactly 2 servers outside the peak.
fix: Add one line: "Assume off-peak load stays below 2 × 60 = 120 requests per second, so the minimum of 2 servers is enough outside the peak."

problem: "A warm pool reduces boot delay but costs for stopped capacity" is loose. A fully stopped server is not billed for compute time in most clouds; the cost is for the storage and reserved resources that are kept ready.
fix: "A warm pool reduces boot delay but you still pay for the storage and resources kept ready for the stopped servers."

problem: "stop paying when it is gone" is unclear; a beginner may read "gone" as the data being deleted rather than the resource being released.
fix: "On-demand computing means a user can ask for a resource when it is needed and stop paying when it is released."
